{{Short description|Exactly solvable model of coupled oscillators}}
The '''Kuramoto model''' (or '''Kuramoto–Daido model'''), first proposed by {{nihongo|[[Yoshiki Kuramoto]]|蔵本 由紀|Kuramoto Yoshiki}},<ref>{{cite book |last = Kuramoto | first = Yoshiki |title = Lecture Notes in Physics, International Symposium on Mathematical Problems in Theoretical Physics |volume = 39 | publisher = Springer-Verlag, New York | page = 420 |year = 1975 |editor= H. Araki}}</ref><ref>{{cite book | author = Kuramoto Y | title = Chemical Oscillations, Waves, and Turbulence | publisher = New York, NY: Springer-Verlag | year = 1984 }}</ref> is a [[mathematical model]] used in describing [[synchronization]]. More specifically, it is a model for the behavior of a large set of coupled [[oscillators]].<ref name=Strogatz-2000>{{cite journal | last = Strogatz | first = Steven H. | author-link = Steven Strogatz| title = From Kuramoto to Crawford: Exploring the onset of synchronization in populations of coupled oscillators | journal = Physica D | volume = 143 | issue = 1–4 | pages = 1–20 | year = 2000 | bibcode = 2000PhyD..143....1S | doi = 10.1016/S0167-2789(00)00094-4 | s2cid = 16668746 | url = https://www.stevenstrogatz.com/articles/from-kuramoto-to-crawford-exploring-the-onset-of-synchronization-in-populations-of-coupled-oscillators-pdf
| access-date = 2024-01-04| doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Acebrón | first1 = Juan A. | last2 = Bonilla | first2 = L. L. | last3 = Vicente | first3 = Pérez | last4 = Conrad | first4 = J. | last5 = Ritort | first5 = Félix | last6 = Spigler | first6 = Renato | journal = Reviews of Modern Physics | pages = 137–185 | title = The Kuramoto model: A simple paradigm for synchronization phenomena | url = http://scala.uc3m.es/publications_MANS/PDF/finalKura.pdf | volume = 77 | issue = 1 | year = 2005|bibcode = 2005RvMP...77..137A |doi = 10.1103/RevModPhys.77.137 | hdl = 2445/12768 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> Its formulation was motivated by the behavior of systems of [[chemical]] and [[biological process|biological]] oscillators, and it has found widespread applications in areas such as [[Neural oscillation#Mathematical description|neuroscience]]<ref name="Understanding the dynamics of biolo">{{cite journal | last1 = Bick | first1 = Christian | last2 = Goodfellow | first2 = Marc | last3 = Laing | first3 = Carlo R. | last4 = Martens | first4 = Erik A. | journal = Journal of Mathematical Neuroscience | page = 9 | title = Understanding the dynamics of biological and neural oscillator networks through exact mean-field reductions: a review | volume = 10 | issue = 1 | year = 2020 | doi = 10.1186/s13408-020-00086-9 |arxiv=1902.05307 | pmid = 32462281 | pmc = 7253574 | doi-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cumin | first1 = D. | last2 = Unsworth | first2 = C. P. | doi = 10.1016/j.physd.2006.12.004 | issue = 2 | journal = Physica D | pages = 181–196 | title = Generalising the Kuromoto model for the study of neuronal synchronisation in the brain | volume = 226 | year = 2007 | bibcode = 2007PhyD..226..181C | hdl = 2292/2666 | hdl-access = free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.3389/fnhum.2010.00190 |pmid=21151358 |pmc=2995481 |vauthors=Breakspear M, Heitmann S, Daffertshofer A | title = Generative models of cortical oscillations: Neurobiological implications of the Kuramoto model | journal = Front Hum Neurosci | volume = 4 | issue = 190 | year = 2010 |page=190 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi = 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2013.11.047 |vauthors=Cabral J, Luckhoo H, Woolrich M, Joensson M, Mohseni H, Baker A, Kringelbach ML, Deco G | title = Exploring mechanisms of spontaneous functional connectivity in MEG: How delayed network interactions lead to structured amplitude envelopes of band-pass filtered oscillations | journal = NeuroImage | volume = 90 | pages = 423–435 | year = 2014 | pmid=24321555| doi-access = free | hdl = 10230/23081 | hdl-access = free }}</ref> and oscillating flame dynamics.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Sivashinsky | first1 = G.I. | doi = 10.1080/00102207708946779 |issue = 3–4 | journal = Combust. Sci. Technol. | pages = 137–146 | title = Diffusional-thermal theory of cellular flames | volume = 15 | year = 1977 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Forrester | first1 = D.M. | doi = 10.1038/srep16994  | doi-access = free| pmid = 26582365 | pmc = 4652215 | journal = Scientific Reports | article-number = 16994  | title = Arrays of coupled chemical oscillators | volume = 5 | year = 2015 |bibcode = 2015NatSR...516994F | arxiv = 1606.01556 }}</ref> Kuramoto was quite surprised when the behavior of some physical systems, namely coupled arrays of [[Josephson junctions]], followed his model.<ref>Steven Strogatz, ''Sync: The Emerging Science of Spontaneous Order'', Hyperion, 2003.</ref>

The model makes several assumptions, including that there is weak coupling, that the oscillators are identical or nearly identical, and that interactions depend sinusoidally on the phase difference between each pair of objects.

== Definition ==
[[File:KuramotoModelPhaseLocking.ogv|thumb|upright=1.1|Phase locking in the Kuramoto model]]

In the most popular version of the Kuramoto model, each of the oscillators is considered to have its own intrinsic [[natural frequency]] <math>\omega_i</math>, and each is coupled equally to all other oscillators. Surprisingly, this fully [[Nonlinear system|nonlinear]] model can be solved exactly in the limit of infinite oscillators, ''N''&nbsp;→ ∞;<ref name="Understanding the dynamics of biolo"/> alternatively, using self-consistency arguments, one may obtain steady-state solutions of the order parameter.<ref name=Strogatz-2000 /> 
The most popular form of the model has the following governing equations:
<math display="block">
 \frac{d \theta_i}{d t} = \omega_i + \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N K_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i), \qquad i = 1 \ldots N,
</math>
where the system is composed of ''N'' limit-cycle oscillators, with phases <math>\theta_i</math> and coupling constant ''K''.

Noise can be added to the system. In that case, the original equation is altered to
<math display="block">
 \frac{d \theta_i}{d t} = \omega_i + \zeta_i + \dfrac{K}{N} \sum_{j=1}^N \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i),
</math>
where <math>\zeta_i</math> is the fluctuation and a function of time. If the noise is considered to be white noise, then
<math display="block">
 \langle\zeta_i(t)\rangle = 0,
</math>
<math display="block">
 \langle\zeta_i(t) \zeta_j(t')\rangle = 2D\delta_{ij}\delta(t - t'),
</math> 
with <math>D</math> denoting the strength of noise.

== Transformation ==
The transformation that allows this model to be solved exactly (at least in the ''N'' → ∞ limit) is as follows:

Define the "order" parameters ''r'' and ''ψ'' as
:<math>re^{i \psi} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{i \theta_j}  </math>.
Here ''r'' represents the phase-[[coherence (physics)|coherence]] of the population of oscillators and ''ψ'' indicates the average phase. Substituting in the equation gives
:<math> \frac{d \theta_i}{d t} = \omega_i + K r \sin(\psi-\theta_i) </math>.

Thus the oscillators' equations are no longer explicitly coupled; instead the order parameters govern the behavior. A further transformation is usually done, to a rotating frame in which the statistical average of phases over all oscillators is zero (i.e. <math>\psi=0</math>). Finally, the governing equation becomes
:<math> \frac{d \theta_i}{d t} = \omega_i - K r \sin(\theta_i) </math>.

== Large ''N'' limit ==
Now consider the case as ''N'' tends to infinity. Take the distribution of intrinsic natural frequencies as ''g''(''ω'') (assumed [[normalization constant|normalized]]).  Then assume that the density of oscillators at a given phase ''θ'', with given natural frequency ''ω'', at time ''t'' is <math>\rho(\theta, \omega, t)</math>.  Normalization requires that 
:<math> \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \rho(\theta, \omega, t) \, d \theta = 1. </math>

The [[continuity equation]] for oscillator density will be 
:<math> \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}[\rho v] = 0, </math>
where ''v'' is the [[drift velocity]] of the oscillators given by taking the infinite-''N'' limit in the transformed governing equation, such that 
:<math> \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial t} + \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta}[\rho \omega + \rho K r \sin(\psi-\theta)] = 0. </math>

Finally, the definition of the order parameters must be rewritten for the continuum (infinite ''N'') limit. <math>\theta_i</math> must be replaced by its ensemble average (over all <math>\omega</math>) and the sum must be replaced by an integral, to give
:<math> 
r e^{i \psi} = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} e^{i \theta} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \rho(\theta, \omega, t) g(\omega) \, d \omega \, d \theta.
</math>

=== Solutions for the large ''N'' limit ===
The [[Coherence (physics)|incoherent]] state with all oscillators drifting randomly corresponds to the solution <math>\rho = 1/(2\pi)</math>. In that case <math>r = 0</math>, and there is no coherence among the oscillators. They are uniformly distributed across all possible phases, and the population is in a statistical [[steady-state]] (although individual oscillators continue to change phase in accordance with their intrinsic ''ω'').

When coupling ''K'' is sufficiently strong, a fully synchronized solution is possible. In the fully synchronized state, all the oscillators share a common frequency, although their phases can be different.

A solution for the case of partial synchronization yields a state in which only some oscillators (those near the ensemble's mean natural frequency) synchronize; other oscillators drift incoherently. Mathematically, the state has
:<math>\rho = \delta\left(\theta - \psi - \arcsin\left(\frac{\omega}{K r}\right)\right)</math> 
for locked oscillators, and
:<math>\rho = \frac{\rm{normalization \; constant}}{(\omega - K r \sin(\theta - \psi))}</math>
for drifting oscillators. The cutoff occurs when <math>|\omega| < K r </math>.

When <math>g</math> is unimodal and symmetric, then a stable state solution for the system is <math display="block">r=rK \int_{-\pi / 2}^{\pi / 2} \cos ^2 \theta g(K r \sin \theta) d \theta</math>As coupling increases, there is a critical value <math>K_c = 2/\pi g(0)</math> such that when <math>K < K_c</math>, the long-term average of <math>r=0</math>, but when <math>K= K_c(1+\mu)</math>, where <math>\mu > 0</math> is small, then <math>r \approx \sqrt{\frac{16}{\pi K_{\mathrm{c}}^3}} \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{-g^{\prime \prime}(0)}}</math>.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Strogatz |first=Steven H. |title=Frontiers in Mathematical Biology |chapter=Norbert Wiener's Brain Waves |date=1994 |editor-last=Levin |editor-first=Simon A. |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-642-50124-1_7 |series=Lecture Notes in Biomathematics |volume=100 |language=en |location=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |pages=122–138 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-50124-1_7 |isbn=978-3-642-50124-1}}</ref><ref name=Strogatz-2000/>

== Small ''N'' cases ==
When N is small, the solutions given above breaks down, as the continuum approximation cannot be used.

The N=2 case is trivial. In the rotating frame <math>\omega_1 = -\omega_2</math>, and so the system is described exactly by the angle between the two oscillators: <math>\Delta \theta = \theta_1 - \theta_2</math>. When <math>K < K_c = 2|\omega_1|</math>, the angle cycles around the circle (that is, the fast oscillator keeps lapping around the slow oscillator). When <math>K > K_c</math>, the angle falls into a stable attractor (that is, the two oscillators lock in phase). Similarly, the state space of the N=3 case is a 2-dimensional torus, and so the system evolves as a flow on the 2-torus, which cannot be chaotic.

Chaos first occurs when N=4. For some settings of <math>\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3, K</math>, the system has a [[strange attractor]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Maistrenko |first1=Yuri L. |last2=Popovych |first2=Oleksandr V. |last3=Tass |first3=Peter A. |title=Chaotic Attractor in the Kuramoto Model |date=November 2005 |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0218127405014155 |journal=International Journal of Bifurcation and Chaos |language=en |volume=15 |issue=11 |pages=3457–3466 |doi=10.1142/S0218127405014155 |bibcode=2005IJBC...15.3457M |issn=0218-1274|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

A related case for N=2 is the [[circle map]] or [[phase-locked loop]]. In this model, one of the oscillators is driven at a fixed frequency (and thus no longer free to vary), while the other, weakly coupled to the driver, is free to spin arbitrarily.

== Connection to Hamiltonian systems ==
The dissipative Kuramoto model is contained<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Witthaut | first1 = Dirk | last2 = Timme | first2 = Marc | title = Kuramoto Dynamics in Hamiltonian Systems | journal = Phys. Rev. E | volume=90 | issue = 3 | article-number = 032917 | doi =  10.1103/PhysRevE.90.032917| pmid = 25314514 | year = 2014|arxiv = 1305.1742 |bibcode = 2014PhRvE..90c2917W | s2cid = 7510614 }}</ref> in certain conservative [[Hamiltonian mechanics|Hamiltonian systems]] with [[Hamilton function|Hamiltonian]] of the form
:<math>  \mathcal{H}(q_1,\ldots, q_N, p_1, \ldots, p_N) = \sum_{i = 1}^N \frac{\omega_i}{2} (q_i^2 +  p_i^2) + \frac{K}{4N} \sum_{i,j = 1}^{N}
       (q_i p_j - q_j p_i) ( q_j^2 + p_j^2 - q_i^2 - p_i^2 )  </math>  
After a [[canonical transformation]] to action-angle variables with actions <math> I_i =  \left( q_i^2 + p_i^2 \right)/2 </math> and angles (phases) <math>
  \phi_i = \mathrm{arctan} \left( q_i/p_i \right) </math>, exact Kuramoto dynamics emerges on [[Invariant manifold|invariant manifolds]] of constant <math> I_i \equiv I </math>. With the transformed Hamiltonian 
:<math>  \mathcal{H'}(I_1, \ldots I_N, \phi_1 \ldots, \phi_N) = \sum_{i = 1}^N \omega_i I_i  
       - \frac{K}{N} \sum_{i = 1}^{N} \sum_{j = 1}^{N} 
              \sqrt{I_j I_i} (I_j  - I_i) \sin(\phi_j - \phi_i),  </math>

Hamilton's equation of motion become 
:<math>
    \frac{d I_i}{dt} = - \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}'}{\partial \phi_i} 
  = - \frac{2 K}{N} \sum_{k=1}^N \sqrt{I_k I_i} (I_k - I_i) \cos(\phi_k - \phi_i)
</math>
and
:<math>
 \frac{d \phi_i}{dt} = \frac{\partial \mathcal{H}'}{\partial I_i}
  = \omega_i + \frac{K}{N}   
        \sum_{k=1}^N \left[ 2 \sqrt{I_i I_k} \sin(\phi_k - \phi_i)  \right.
       \left. +
          \sqrt{I_k/I_i} (I_k - I_i) \sin(\phi_k - \phi_i) \right] .
</math>
So the manifold with <math> I_j = I </math> is invariant because <math>  \frac{d I_i}{dt} = 0 </math> and the phase dynamics <math> \frac{d \phi_i}{dt} </math> becomes the dynamics of the Kuramoto model (with the same coupling constants for <math> I = 1/2 </math>). The class of Hamiltonian systems characterizes certain quantum-classical systems including [[Bose–Einstein condensate]]s.

== Variations of the models ==
[[File:Spatial synchronization patterns in variants of the Kuramoto Model.png|thumb|upright=1.1|right|Distinct synchronization patterns in a two-dimensional array of Kuramoto-like oscillators with differing phase interaction functions and spatial coupling topologies.  (A) Pinwheels. (B) Waves. (C) Chimeras. (D) Chimeras and waves combined. Color scale indicates oscillator phase.]]
There are a number of types of variations that can be applied to the original model presented above. Some models change the [[Topological space|topological structure]], others allow for heterogeneous weights, and other changes are more related to models that are inspired by the Kuramoto model but do not have the same functional form.

=== Variations of network topology ===
Beside the original model, which has an all-to-all topology, a sufficiently dense [[Complex Network|complex network]]-like topology is amenable to the mean-field treatment used in the solution of the original model<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Rodrigues | first1 = F. A. | last2 = Peron | first2 = T. K. | last3 = Jie | first3 = P.|last4 = Kurths | first4 = J.| title = The Kuramoto model in complex networks | journal = Physics Reports | volume=610 | issue=1 | pages = 1–98 | doi = 10.1016/j.physrep.2015.10.008 | year = 2016| arxiv = 1511.07139 | bibcode = 2016PhR...610....1R | s2cid = 119290926 }}</ref> (see [[#Transformation|Transformation]] and [[#Large N limit|Large ''N'' limit]] above for more info). Network topologies such as rings and coupled populations support chimera states.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Abrams | first1 = D. M. | last2 = Strogatz | first2 = S. H. | title = Chimera states for coupled oscillators | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 93 |issue = 17 | article-number = 174102 | year = 2004|doi=10.1103/physrevlett.93.174102 | pmid = 15525081 |arxiv = nlin/0407045 |bibcode = 2004PhRvL..93q4102A | s2cid = 8615112 }}</ref> One also may ask for the behavior of models in which there are intrinsically local, like one-dimensional topologies which the chain and the ring are prototypical examples. In such topologies, in which the coupling is not scalable according to 1/''N'', it is not possible to apply the canonical mean-field approach, so one must rely upon case-by-case analysis, making use of symmetries whenever it is possible, which may give basis for abstraction of general principles of solutions.

Uniform synchrony, waves and spirals can readily be observed in two-dimensional Kuramoto networks with diffusive local coupling. The stability of waves in these models can be determined analytically using the methods of Turing stability analysis.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Kazanci | first1 = F. | last2 = Ermentrout | first2 = B. | title = Pattern formation in an array of oscillators with electrical and chemical coupling | journal = SIAM J Appl Math | volume=67 | issue = 2 | pages = 512–529 | doi = 10.1137/060661041 | year = 2006| citeseerx = 10.1.1.140.1020 }}</ref> Uniform synchrony tends to be stable when the local coupling is everywhere positive whereas waves arise when the long-range connections are negative (inhibitory surround coupling). Waves and synchrony are connected by a topologically distinct branch of solutions known as ripple.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Heitmann | first1 = S. | last2 = Gong | first2 = P. | last3 = Breakspear | first3 = M. | title = A computational role for bistability and traveling waves in motor cortex | journal = Front Comput Neurosci | volume=6 | issue=67 | page = 67 | doi = 10.3389/fncom.2012.00067 | pmid = 22973223 | year = 2012| pmc = 3438483 | doi-access = free }}</ref> These are low-amplitude spatially-periodic deviations that emerge from the uniform state (or the wave state) via a [[Hopf bifurcation]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Heitmann | first1 = S. | last2 = Ermentrout | first2 = B. |title = Synchrony, waves and ripple in spatially coupled Kuramoto oscillators with Mexican hat connectivity | journal = Biological Cybernetics | pages = 1–15 | doi = 10.1007/s00422-015-0646-6 | pmid = 25677527 | year = 2015 | volume=109| issue = 3 | s2cid = 18561153 }}</ref> The existence of ripple solutions was predicted (but not observed) by Wiley, Strogatz and [[Michelle Girvan|Girvan]],<ref name=":0">{{cite journal | last1 = Wiley | first1 = D. | last2 = Strogatz | first2 = S. | last3 = Girvan | first3 = M. |author3-link= Michelle Girvan | title = The size of the sync basin | volume = 16 | issue = 1 | journal = Chaos | page = 015103 | doi = 10.1063/1.2165594 | pmid = 16599769 | year = 2006|bibcode = 2006Chaos..16a5103W | s2cid = 21173189 }}</ref> who called them multi-twisted q-states.

The topology on which the Kuramoto model is studied can be made adaptive<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Eom | first1 = Y.-H. | last2 = Boccaletti | first2 = S. | last3 = Caldarelli | first3 = G. | title = Concurrent enhancement of percolation and synchronization in adaptive networks | volume = 7 | journal = Scientific Reports | page = 015103 | doi = 10.1038/srep27111  | doi-access = free| pmid = 27251577 | pmc = 4890019 | year = 2016 | article-number = 27111 | arxiv = 1511.05468 | bibcode = 2016NatSR...627111E }}</ref> by use of [[Fitness model (network theory)|fitness model]] showing enhancement of synchronization and [[neuropercolation|percolation]] in a self-organised way.

A graph with the minimal degree at least <math>d_\text{min} \ge 0.5\,n</math> will be connected nevertheless for a graph to synchronize a little more it is required for such case it is known that there is critical connectivity threshold <math>\mu_c</math> such that any graph on <math>n</math> nodes with minimum degree <math>d_\text{min} \ge \mu_c (n - 1)</math> must globally synchronise.for <math>n</math> large enough. The minimum<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite arXiv |last=Canale |first=Eduardo A. |date=2022 |title=From weighted to unweighted graphs in Synchronizing Graph Theory |class=math.CO |eprint=2209.06362}}</ref> maximum<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kassabov |first1=Martin |last2=Strogatz |first2=Steven H. |last3=Townsend |first3=Alex |date=2021-07-01 |title=Sufficiently dense Kuramoto networks are globally synchronizing |url=https://pubs.aip.org/cha/article/31/7/073135/342231/Sufficiently-dense-Kuramoto-networks-are-globally |journal=Chaos: An Interdisciplinary Journal of Nonlinear Science |language=en |volume=31 |issue=7 |page=073135 |doi=10.1063/5.0057659 |pmid=34340322 |arxiv=2105.11406 |bibcode=2021Chaos..31g3135K |s2cid=235166315 |issn=1054-1500}}</ref> are known to lie between <math>0.6875\le \mu_c\le 0.75</math>.

Similarly it is known that [[Erdős–Rényi model|Erdős-Rényi graphs]] with edge probability precisely <math>p=(1+\epsilon)\ln (n)/n</math> as <math>n</math> goes to infinity will be connected and it has been conjectured<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ling |first1=Shuyang |last2=Xu |first2=Ruitu |last3=Bandeira |first3=Afonso S. |date=January 2019 |title=On the Landscape of Synchronization Networks: A Perspective from Nonconvex Optimization |url=https://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/18M1217644 |journal=SIAM Journal on Optimization |language=en |volume=29 |issue=3 |pages=1879–1907 |arxiv=1809.11083 |doi=10.1137/18M1217644 |issn=1052-6234 |s2cid=53067184}}</ref> that this value is too the number at which these random graphs undergo synchronization which a 2022 preprint claims to have proved.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Abdalla |first1=Pedro |last2=Bandeira |first2=Afonso S. |last3=Kassabov |first3=Martin |last4=Souza |first4=Victor |last5=Strogatz |first5=Steven H. |last6=Townsend |first6=Alex |date=2022 |title=Expander graphs are globally synchronising |class=math.CO |eprint=2210.12788}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Sloman |first=Leila |date=24 July 2023 |title=New Proof Shows That 'Expander' Graphs Synchronize |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/new-proof-shows-that-expander-graphs-synchronize-20230724/ |website=[[Quanta Magazine]]}}</ref>

=== Variations of network topology and network weights: from vehicle coordination to brain synchronization ===
[[File:Wesphysdemo - Synchronized Metronomes.webm|thumb|upright=1.1|[[Metronome]]s, initially out of phase, synchronize through small motions of the base on which they are placed. This system has been shown to be equivalent to the Kuramoto model.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Pantaleone |first1=James |title=Synchronization of metronomes |journal=American Journal of Physics |date=October 2002 |volume=70 |issue=10 |pages=992–1000 |doi=10.1119/1.1501118 |bibcode=2002AmJPh..70..992P |url=http://www.math.pitt.edu/~bard/classes/mth3380/syncpapers/metronome.pdf}}</ref>]]
Some works in the control community have focused on the Kuramoto model on networks and with heterogeneous weights (i.e. the interconnection strength between any two oscillators can be arbitrary). The dynamics of this model reads as follows:
:<math> \frac{d \theta_i}{d t} = \omega_i + \sum_{j=1}^{N} a_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i), \qquad i = 1 \ldots N</math>
where <math>a_{ij}</math> is a nonzero positive real number if oscillator <math>j</math> is connected to oscillator <math>i</math>. Such model allows for a more realistic study of, e.g., power grids,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Filatrella |first1=G. |last2=Nielsen |first2=A.H. |last3=Pedersen |first3=N.F. |title=Analysis of a power grid using a Kuramoto-like model |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjb/e2008-00098-8 |journal=The European Physical Journal B |publication-date=2008 |volume=61 |issue=4 |pages=485–491 |doi=10.1140/epjb/e2008-00098-8 |arxiv=0705.1305 }}</ref> flocking, schooling, and vehicle coordination.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Dorfler | first1 = F. | last2 = Bullo | first2 = F. | issue = 6 | journal = Automatica | pages = 1539–1564 | title = Synchronization in complex networks of phase oscillators: A survey | volume = 50 | year = 2014 |doi = 10.1016/j.automatica.2014.04.012 }}</ref> In the work from Dörfler and colleagues, several theorems provide rigorous conditions for phase and frequency synchronization of this model. Further studies, motivated by experimental observations in neuroscience, focus on deriving analytical conditions for cluster synchronization of heterogeneous Kuramoto oscillators on arbitrary network topologies.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Menara | first1 = T. | last2 = Baggio | first2 = G. | last3 = Bassett | first3 = D. | last4 = Pasqualetti | first4 = F. | journal = IEEE Transactions on Control of Network Systems | pages = 302–314 | volume = 7 | issue = 1 | title = Stability Conditions for Cluster Synchronizations in Networks of Heterogeneous Kuramoto Oscillators | year = 2020 | doi = 10.1109/TCNS.2019.2903914 | arxiv = 1806.06083 | s2cid = 73729229 }}</ref>

Since the Kuramoto model seems to play a key role in assessing synchronization phenomena in the brain,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Cabral | first1 = J. | last2 = Hugues | first2 = E. | last3 = Sporns | first3 = O. | last4 = Deco | first4 = G. | journal = NeuroImage | volume = 57 | issue = 1| pages = 130–139| title = Role of local network oscillations in resting-state functional connectivity | year = 2011 |doi = 10.1016/j.neuroimage.2011.04.010 | pmid = 21511044 | s2cid = 13959959 }}</ref> theoretical conditions that support empirical findings may pave the way for a deeper understanding of neuronal synchronization phenomena.

=== Variations of the phase interaction function ===
Kuramoto approximated the phase interaction between any two oscillators by its first Fourier component, namely <math>\Gamma(\phi) = \sin(\phi)</math>, where <math>\phi = \theta_j - \theta_i</math>. Better approximations can be obtained by including higher-order Fourier components, 
:<math>\Gamma(\phi) = \sin(\phi) + a_1 \sin(2\phi + b_1) + ... + a_n \sin(2n\phi + b_n)</math>,
where parameters <math>a_i</math> and <math>b_i</math> must be estimated. For example, synchronization among a network of weakly-coupled [[Hodgkin–Huxley model|Hodgkin–Huxley neurons]] can be replicated using coupled oscillators that retain the first four Fourier components of the interaction function.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hansel | first1 = D. | last2 = Mato | first2 = G. | last3 = Meunier | first3 = C | issue = 5 | journal = Europhysics Letters | pages = 367–372 | title = Phase Dynamics for Weakly Coupled Hodgkin-Huxley Neurons | volume = 23 | year = 1993|bibcode = 1993EL.....23..367H |doi = 10.1209/0295-5075/23/5/011 | s2cid = 250884499 }}</ref> The introduction of higher-order phase interaction terms can also induce interesting dynamical phenomena such as partially synchronized states,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Clusella|first1=Pau|last2=Politi|first2=Antonio|last3=Rosenblum|first3=Michael|date=2016|title=A minimal model of self-consistent partial synchrony|journal=New Journal of Physics|language=en|volume=18|issue=9|article-number=093037|doi=10.1088/1367-2630/18/9/093037|issn=1367-2630|bibcode=2016NJPh...18i3037C|arxiv=1607.07178|s2cid=126227664 }}</ref> [[heteroclinic cycle]]s,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Hansel | first1 = D. | last2 = Mato | first2 = G. | last3 = Meunier | first3 = C | title = Clustering and slow switching in globally coupled phase oscillators | journal = Physical Review E | volume = 48 | issue = 5 | pages = 3470–3477 |doi=10.1103/physreve.48.3470 | pmid = 9961005 | year = 1993|bibcode = 1993PhRvE..48.3470H | url = https://hal.science/hal-02387163/file/Hansel1993.pdf }}</ref> and [[Chaos theory|chaotic dynamics]].<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Bick | first1 = C. | last2 = Timme | first2 = M. | last3 = Paulikat | first3 = D. | last4 = Rathlev | first4 = D. | last5 = Ashwin | first5 = P. | title = Chaos in Symmetric Phase Oscillator Networks | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 107 |issue = 24 | article-number = 244101 | year = 2011 | doi = 10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.244101 | pmid = 22243002 | arxiv = 1105.2230 | bibcode = 2011PhRvL.107x4101B | s2cid = 16144737 }}</ref>

== Availability ==
* [https://github.com/annoviko/pyclustering pyclustering] library includes a Python and C++ implementation of the Kuramoto model and its modifications. Also the library consists of oscillatory networks (for [[cluster analysis]], pattern recognition, [[graph coloring]], [[image segmentation]]) that are based on the Kuramoto model and phase oscillator.
